subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OP THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The sifbamendlment which has been moved to the 'budget brings up the whale question of better trade relations between this country and the motherland, and concerns boitlh British preferential trade and inter-rmiperial trade. With all due respect to the government, I would ask if they think the people of this country are satisfied to allow the present condition of affairs to continue and for us to go on importing from the United States every year $900,000,000 worth of high-priced manufactured goods, while our own sons and daughters have to leave our shores in large numbers to seek employment in the United States. Conditions in the old land are very similar.
The subamendment urges upon the consideration of the government an immediate and substantial increase in the British preference. The subamendment reads:
That the amendment be amended by striking out all the words after "house" and substituting therefor the following:	_	_
"urges upon the government the consideration of an immediate and substantial increase of the British preference as a step towards freer trade relations between Canada and other nations."
In other words, the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer), who has moved this amendment, is following the line which was suggested by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), that when we are shut out from the United States market we should look elsewhere. The hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer) referred to Russia as a country to which we might look for increased trade when we are virtually kicked out of the United States by the new tariff changes and he also spoke about Great Britain. The tariff policy of the United States is based on the principle that charity begins at home. That principle in fiscal matters has been enunciated by all the great presidents of the United States from Lincoln down to Roosevelt and Hoover. They have always taken the stand that in matters of tariff charity begins at home, that the
home market belongs to their own manufacturers and working men. But unfortunately for this country the government at Ottawa seems to be asleep. It has given preferential treatment to twenty-eight countries bordering on the seven seas; but when it comes to the motherland, oh, what a difference. If Canada is to be a self-respecting country the government should write an economic note instead of a peace note to the government of the United States to the effect that we can no longer continue-the present one-sided reciprocity under which we buy nine hundred million dollars' worth of high-priced manufactured goods from our neighbours and pay for them with our raw materials; that we can no longer squander the capital and labour of future generations in this manner; that if the United States government desires to enter into an equitable reciprocity arrangement with us, it must do so with all convenient speed, otherwise we shall take immediate steps to put in operation such a national policy as will conserve our raw materials for our own manufacturers and our own workmen and to deal with the United States as they deal with us by making our duties the equal of theirs and intimating to them that we will have a proper reciprocity or none.
A few days ago the Prime Minister said that in dealing with the United States we must keep cool heads. Well, it seems to me that the government has not only a cool head, it has got cold feet too. No self-respecting country in the world would tolerate what Canada has had to put up with in the past in the shape of the various tariff barriers which have been erected by our neighbours. The government of the United States is well able to take care of the economic and other interests of its own people. Would that we had a government as fully alive to the interests, economic and otherwise, of the Canadian people; then our working men would be more fairly dealt with. This government turns a deaf ear to any proposal to give really preferential treatment to Great Britain. Within the confines of the British Empire there are several hundred millions of people, and we should put into force a system of interimperial trade. That day cannot come too soon. The Prime Minister may know Ottawa, he may know the White House; but the leader of the opposition knows all Canada and all England, he knows what Canada and the empire need-an economic tariff. He knows that in an imperial fiscal sense charity begins at home. Instead of the Prime Minister talking about our keeping cool heads and giving the United States a chance, why does he not take steps to give Canada a
The Budget-Mr. Church

chance, the British Empire a chance, interimperial trade a chance? We have had too much government from Washington and altogether too little from Ottawa in a fiscal sense.
This government has established a Canadian embassy at Washington. It would seem to me, judging from the speeches delivered in the United States by our splendid minister extraordinary-and I say he is extraordinary -that our embassy is just an agency for boosting pan-American trade at the expense of the British Empire. Only the other day this extraordinary plenipotentiary took the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) in hand-a minister who is the "glass of fashion "-and walked him up to the White House to see President Hoover. It was also announced that our minister plenipotentiary down there would be happy to introduce any other member of the House of Commons to Washington and to the present occupant of the White House. I do not know if I am likely to be in Washington any time this year, but if I am our minister extraordinary will not have an opportunity of walking me up to the White House. Of course, I may not be the " glass of fashion " like some hon. gentlemen who are driven around in ten-thousand-dollar high-powered cars. In 1925 I accompanied Mr. Hoover and his friends over the Welland canal and St. Lawrence waterway for two days and gave a banquet in Toronto to him and about two hundred other people in connection with the harbour development there.
From my contact with him then I became convinced that he is a man of exceptional ability, and I am sure he will prove himself to be one of the greatest presidents that the United States has ever had. But besides his intimate knowledge of his own country he knows the British Empire as no other American knows it. He lived for 23 years in the British Empire. Of course, he recognizes the right of every country to shape its own fiscal policy so as to ensure markets for its own people and work for its own working men. I know he is very friendly in his attitude towards the British Empire and wishes to see it become even more abundantly prosperous.
Last year we were visited by the Prime Minister of Great Britain, Mr. Baldwin, by Mr. Amery, the Secretary of State for the Colonies, and last but not least, by Mr. Chamberlain, Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, and by Sir William Clark. Each of them urged Canada to stay within the British Empire to foster inter-imperial trade, and to buy in other parts of the empire such products

as she did not produce herself. No one can take exception to their advice. It is good Conservative doctrine. But what can we expect from this government? In reply to the kid-glove platitudes of the hon. Minister of Justice, I submit that we are not retaliating against the United States if we keep on buying nine hundred million dollars' worth of goods, notwithstanding the avowed purpose of the United States government still further to raise its tariff barriers against Canada. The policy of this government seems to be, if they smite you on the left cheek, turn to them your right. Talk about keeping coo! heads! Every member of the government from the Prime Minister downwards seems to have cold feet. They refuse to do anything for the motherland in the way of an adequate British preference that would expand our trade with the British people and would mean diverting to them the thirty or forty per cent of trade and of money that is now going to the United States for high-priced goods. The policy of the government has made us hewers of wood and drawers of water for the United States. What does this government care about a proper British preference which will assist the motherland? Hon. gentlemen opposite care nothing about it. They are indifferent to farm relief and rural depopulation in this country, indifferent to unemployment so long as they can continue their policy of semi-free trade with the United States. They have simply pursued a policy of laissez faire towards the British Empire and the motherland and the British preference. The next general election cannot come too soon in the interests of this country; it will, I believe, put an end to this policy on the part of the government. Tens of thousands of tons of Welsh coal could be brought to this country, providing employment for the miners in the old country, and thus implementing the British preference; but instead of that the government are content to have this country send millions of dollars over to the United States to provide employment for the miners of Pennsylvania. It was not free trade and Cobdenism that made England the great country she became; it was the union of coal and steel one hundred and fifty years ago. That was what made England great, and if the government in office here have the interests of the Canadian people at heart they will inaugurate a policy which will have for its object the development of the coal and steel industry of this Dominion and the encouragement of preferential interimperial trade. The government do not seem to realize that this country is a heritage which must 'be safeguarded for those who are to follow. Mussolini, the great leader of Italy,

The Budget-Division
speaking of a country, says: A country does not belong to those who inhabit it to-day; it is an inheritance from the past, a possession for the present, and a trust for the future. The same thing applies to Canada. But what do hon. gentlemen opposite care about the future prosperity of Canada or the trust they hold to-day to foster inter-imperial trade and advance our empire.
The policy of this government, in their attitude towards Canadian development and Canada's relations with the motherland and with the British Empire generally, seems to be twofold: First, that nothing that can be bought in the United States should be made in Canada, especially in eastern Canada ; and, secondly, that everything that cannot be bought in the United States shall be imported from continental Europe, preferably Germany and not from England. That is the preferential policy of the present government. The Conservative party on the other hand believes in a tariff which will, in the first place, develop the industries of this country and, after that, promote trade within the empire. The government are wasting a lot of money on research. The first thing is to search and research for a proper tariff policy and dig up a policy that will help the British Empire, preserve our markets and our work for our own people, and encourage the manufacturing industries of Canada. So far as encouraging trade within the empire is concerned, and particularly assisting the_ mother country, this government's policy may be called "I'm alone." The Prime Minister talks about keeping a cool head; he says we must have a coolheaded policy with the United States. That is a favourite expression of the Prime Minister's. His policy is full of doubts and fears and "ifs" and "buts," provisos and whereases and wherefores, and that he calls keeping a cool head. Well, the government's policy towards the mother country has been very cool; the mother country has always got a very cool reception from this government.

One of the difficulties in connection with an amendment of this kind, in common with all amendments proposed in this house, is that everyone uses his own method of interpreting it. The other day the Prime Minister referred bo this amendment rather extensively, and I think he told the house that it meant more protection, which I understand to mean increases in the tariff. He went on to say that in 1921 the Conservatives appealed to the country on protection and were defeated; that they appealed again in 1925 and in 1926 and got what he said was a knock-out blow somewhat similar to the blow that was given protection in Great Britain about 1905.
The Prime Minister then went on to say that since 1926 protection had -been creeping about in Canada under " modest and belittling pseudonyms," and he instanced this amendment which used the participle " protecting " instead of the substantive word " protection ". However, I think the Prime Minister forgot one

The Budget-Mr. Kennedy
or two other pseudonyms such as "freer trade" and "lower tariff" which have been applied by himself and his own party to what we have in Canada to-day, which without question is a protective policy. If protection received a knock-out blow in the election of 1926, in my judgment there has been no evidence of it in the three budgets which have been presented in this house since that election.
Does the Conservative policy mean, or has it always meant, increasing the tariff? I know it is possible to quote some Conservatives in the affirmative on that question. The Prime Minister referred the other day to the great increase in agricultural production in Canada during the past few years, the increase in acreage and the increase in yield. 1 believe that the Conservative government, or the Union government, was responsible to a large extent for encouraging that increase in production when some years ago it took the duty of small farm tractors.
I do not believe any one reduction in the duty on agricultural machinery has done more to increase production in western Canada than the removal of the duty on small tractors.
I do not wish to take up the time of the house by quoting the speech of the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington (Mr. Edwards), who placed on Hansard at page 956 a list of some reductions brought into effect by the Conservatives. While I am not willing to accept the statement of the Prime Minister the other day as being the correct interpretation of this policy, or the extreme statements made on the other side as to what the Liberal policy means, I think we should remember that the policy of the Conservatives has been followed very closely by the Liberals during the last seven years. I think that is a safer guide than the interpretation given by some Liberals and even by some Conservatives as to the meaning of this amendment. After all, is there any harm in a party which says " if we must protect certain individuals in Canada we must protect everyone "? Surely that is the only logical position for any party to take that adopts protection as a policy if they undertake to protect some people they should go the whole way and protect everyone, as far as that can be done. That is much more logical than promising to abolish protection while giving protection to some and not giving it to others.
The farmers of Canada has not been greatly benefited either by increases or reductions in the tariff. To-day in Canada there are some farmers who believe that the tariff should be increased; they want it increased on their goods because they believe it will mean increased prices to them. On the other hand
there are some farmers who have taken the other view; they want to reduce the tariff. They take that position because they think protection cannot be applied to their industry and they say if that is so it should not be applied to any other industry. However, both groups realize the inequality of the present situation; they desire equality whether it is brought about by increases or decreases in the tariff. In Canada the low, or lower, tariff party, the free traders, or whatever you wish to call them, have been in the ascendancy so far as organized agriculture is concerned, and across the line the farm bloc has been and is protectionist. I want to remind hon. members on both sides of the house that increases in the tariff on agricultural products either in the United States or in Canada do not mean real protection to agriculture. The reason for that, of course, is the impossibility of organized agriculture, to-day taking advantage of a protective tariff. At one time I believe we had a situation in Canada under which a protective tariff on wheat could be taken advantage of; that was when the wheat board was organized in 1919 and if I remember correctly the government of the day passed an order in council compelling the board to sell wheat to the Canadian miller at a price equivalent to that obtained elsewhere less transportation costs. The farm bloc in the United States were successful in 1922 in getting the Fordney-Mc-Cumber tariff passed. In the main, this was a farmers' tariff, and as I do not wish to delay the house longer than necessary, I will not discuss that tariff in detail. I think all the members of the house are sufficiently familiar with the details of that tariff to know that it was chiefly a farmers' tariff. Before it was passed, wheat, cattle and a few other commodities were on the free list, but a duty of 14 to 2 cents per pound was placed against cattle, and a duty of 30 cents per bushel was placed against wheat; by a proclamation of the president, the duty on wheat has since been raised to 42 cents per bushel.
What has been the result in the United States of the application of this increase in duty? I have in my hand a volume entitled Farm Relief, the Annals of the American Academy of Political and Social Science, which summarizes the conditions existing in U.S. agriculture between the years 1920 and 1925, and refers in a general way to the conditions prevailing in later years. I would like to quote a few passages from this volume, beginning with a passage entitled "Farm Prices," which is as follows:
When price data are used, we find an appearance of a depressed condition to-day in the business of farming, as compared with pre-war

The Budget-Mr. Kennedy
years. The index number of the price of farm products averaged 131 in 1927 and varied from 134 to 148 during 1928 on a basis of the prewar half decade as 100. On the same basis the prices paid by farmers varied from 154 to 157. Thus the purchasing power of farm products, at the farm has recently varied from 85 to 95, using the pre-war half decade as a basis of 100.
Another article dealing with mortgage indebtedness, reads as follows:
The total amount of mortgage indebtedness for the country as a whole increased about 13 per cent in the five years ending in 1925. This increase is significant when it is considered that the percentage of the total number of owner-operated farms mortgaged decreased slightly, that a certain amount of indebtedness was wiped out by foreclosure, and that the value of farm real estate decreased nearly 25 per cent.
Naturally, there was a large increase in per cent of mortgage debt to value of farm real estate reporting mortgage, for the United States as a whole from 29.1 per cent in 1920 to 41.9 per cent in 1925. This is indeed a startling change. Moreover, it was marked in every geographic section, even in New England and the middle Atlantic states. In the northwest central group the percentage increased from 26.5 to 44.9; in the single state of Iowa, from 27 per cent to 49.2 per cent.
Thus, while the percentage of farms operated by owners decreased considerably in the major farming areas, the decrease in the percentage of equity owned by the farmers was very much more significant.
The farmers in the United States have an organization known as the American Farm Bureau Federation, and I would' like to quote a few remarks by Mr. Thompson, the president, as follows:
An analysis of the present situation shows that not more than eight hundred thousand farms in this country are being operated today at a profit; eight hundred thousand out of six and a half million.
Full realization of the program of the farm bureau will mean that four and a half million or 80 per cent will be operating at a profit;
That is based on the assumption that the program of the bureau is adopted. In the November Current History is an article entitled "The Farm Problem Made Clear," and I would like to read one or two paragraphs, as follows:
Prices for Farm Products-Taking as a basis of 100 all prices averaged for the five years, 1909-14, the prices for agricultural commodities at the farms which reached a peak of 209 in 1919, dropped to 116 in 1921, and since then have averaged around 130. But prices are relative. The wholesale prices of non-agricultural commodities, on the same basis, reached their peak in 1920 at 241, and since then have been in the neighbourhood of 160 until 1927. For the past year and a half they have been about 152. Thus, the purchasing power of farm products. 100 in 1909-14, reached 107 in 1918, went to 69 in 1921, and has since ranged around 75 to 85, being now about 92. If the com-
parison is made for a period of nearly thirty years, with the prices of 1913 as the basis, it is found that prices for farm products have been lower than those for non-agrieultural products for most of the years during the entire period.
The article goes on to deal with the costs of production, which have been increased on the farm, and also deals with the increase in the prices for farm requirements. Another paragraph entitled " Taxes " reads:
Taxes on farm property increased in the ratio of 100 in 1914 to 250 in 1927, while farm prices increased only to 130. The total amount of the taxes paid on farm property increased during this period from $340,000,000 to $870,000,000. In recent years taxes have taken one-third of the net property income of farmers, and in some areas one-half.
Another paragraph entitled "Debt" reads:
Between 1910 and 1925 the amount of mortgage debt on owner-operated farms increased from $1,726,000,000 to $4,517,000,000; and the ration of debt to value, from 27.3 per cent to 41.9 per cent.
The last paragraph I desire to quote, entitled " Share of National wealth " reads as follows:
The wealth of the nation was perhaps $175,000,000,000 in 1910 and is now possibly $400,000,000,000; farm wealth was $40,000,000,000 in 1910 and is now $60,000,000,000, a dTop from nearly $80,000,000,000 in 1920. Twenty years ago our farmers possessed nearly one-fourth of the national wealth, whereas to-day they have less than one-sixth of it. Moreover, the purchasing power of the farm wealth of the United States is 15 per cent less than it was fifteen years ago.
The United States has evidently gone considerably farther than we have in Canada in the tabulating of the relation between the prices at which the farmer sells his produce and the prices which he has to pay for the different articles he requires. I hope we will have in Canada some day as complete a knowledge of the conditions which prevail here. All the indications we have, however, show that the conditions prevailing in Canada with respect to the relation between the agricultural industries and the other industries are similar to what they are in the United States, and these conditions have not been altered in any substantial degree by any changes which have been made during the last few years in the tariff.
This is a problem for both Canada and the United States and it cannot be solved merely by raising or lowering the tariff one per cent. I think the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) in her speech the other day, showed pretty conclusively that, so far as we have information, conditions in Canada are very similar and anybody who has lived for a while in a city and for a while amongst the farmers and new

The Budget-Mr. Kennedy
settlers in the west, knows that living conditions amongst the farmers are very far from what they ought to be, judged by the standard of even the common people in the towns and cities.
The United States farmers have been attempting to solve the problem of making protection apply to United States agriculture. A great deal of the talk in this house regarding the possible action of the United States at the special session of congress called to deal with farm relief does not, in my judgment, mean very much. I do not believe there is in Canada anyone who is going to criticize seriously the president of the United States for calling a session of congress to deal with the pressing problems confronting that country, or congress for doing anything it feels it must do in order to put the farmers of that country on a parity with the manufacturers and other classes who are getting the benefit of a protective policy. How can we criticize them? They know they have a problem to deal with and surely their responsibility is to their own people, just as ours is to our people in this country. If they feel that is what they must do, we cannot criticize them. If the United States people, by experiment, can find a method of farm relief that will solve the problem over there and will demonstrate that the protective policy can apply to the farmers as well as to the rest, any temporary disadvantage the farmers of Canada might suffer might well be borne if a real solution of the problem could be found. But I doubt it. The people of the United States are carrying on their experiment apparently in a sincere and determined manner, and we will watch the result with much interest.
But what are they asking? Just a few increases in the tariff? Oh, no. The McNary-Haugen bill, as I understand it, is a bill to give the farmers a board and government money to enable them to sell the produce that will be absorbed by the home market in the United States, and to prevent the surplus that they might sell abroad from depressing the price, thus enabling the board which is selling that produce in the United States, to take advantage of any tariff protection or increase in the tariff that is granted. The Conservative party has stated on various occasions that its policy is to prevent people who are getting protection from taking advantage of the consumer, and this is one way whereby we might get equality or something nearer equality than we have to-day. The farmers in the United States and those who are supporting them in congress and elsewhere, are taking the view that the manufacturers take advantage of the
tariff, and while they are not trying to stop them, they simply say that the government, having done that for the manufacturers, is in duty bound to turn around and give the farmers an organization which will enable them to do the same thing in the sale of their products.
In regard to the problem of the export surplus, they are asking for export debentures which amount to a bonus. They are asking also for a readjustment of the taxation burden as between the rural districts and the cities, reducing the farmers' taxes. They are asking for lower interest rates. They are also asking for very much reduced freight rates, and I am sure the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) will be interested in that.

speechtext: My hon. friend will permit me to say that they can stand a great deal of reduction before they are down to our level.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OP THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
About ten cents on a
bushel of wheat. They are also asking for control of production and that no more land be brought under cultivation by irrigation or drainage or any other method until such time as they have this problem solved. They are asking for increases in the tariff. These are the things which the farmers in the United States have laid down as being the protective policy that, in their judgment, is necessary to put agriculture on a par with the other organizations that have been enjoying protection in that country.
They are also taking the view-and they have expressed it-that unless they can get protection for all, so far as they are concerned there must be protection for none. I think I can submit this to both parties; certainly the budget we have to-day is a protective budget. Our policy has been protection for our manufacturers, and if hon. members will examine closely the schedule in the present budget there are no substantial changes downward at all. Of course if the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) Shows us afterwards that there are, and that it means anything to the ultimate consumer, I shall be only too pleased.
The farmers in the United States are also asking for tremendous assistance to their cooperative organizations. This has to do with the organization for the marketing of their produce. While it has been stated time and again that the policy of the government across the way is to help farmers in connection with marketing their crops, there is in the speech of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) one statement which I cannot quite understand. He said, as re-
The Budget-Mr. Kennedy

ported in Hansard of March 14, 1929, at page 948 near the top of the second column:
The Department of Trade and Commerce is not exercised over the sale of such commodities as wheat, because those commodities find their own markets; but we are interested in assisting the sale of manufactured products.
The farmers in Canada will have to raise their voice still louder in order that both the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Trade and Commerce may grasp more thoroughly the fact that while the problems of production are great, a solution of them will not mean very much to our farmers unless along with it we have a real solution of the problem of marketing. While I do not believe the pool or cooperative marketing is going to solve all our problems, it is possibly the biggest thing we can do in the near future to help agriculture in the Dominion of Canada. The wheat pools are well organized, but I think it is generally recognized that the marketing organizations in connection with cattle, which may be affected by an increase in the United States tariff, are in a very poor condition as compared with the wheat organizations. We certainly need to pay a great deal of attention to marketing, and I hope that as a result of the investigation made by the agriculture and colonization committee some arrangement will be come to that will impress upon the government and the department the need for greater marketing opportunities, -and that it will never be possible again for a minister to stand up in the House of Commons and make such a statement. <
I shall! refer to the main motion before I conclude, because I do not wish to make another speech. I for one cannot vote for the budget. If I voted for it I feel that I would be declaring that my votes on the budgets of the last two years were wrong. If I felt that I was wrong in 1927 and 1928, I would get up here and frankly say so, but I still ieel that I was right, because we were working on a policy of lowering the tariffs, and we were advocating at least the collection of our revenue by direct rather than indirect taxation, and in that respect the budgets of 1927 and 1928 both moved in the wrong d'reetion. An amendment was moved by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) to the budget of 1927 to this effect:
Whilst recognizing the advisability of certain minor changes proposed, this house regrets that the budget as presented by the hon. minister of Finance contains no effective provision for the reducing of the high cost of living, in so far as it is due to the protective tariff;

That the budget shows a further departure from the principle of direct and visible taxation based on ability to pay;
And further, that no systematic effort is being made to reduce our national debt, the interest on which absorbs so large a proportion of the revenues of the Dominion.
Then last year I supported an amendment to the budget moved by the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Fansher), reading as follows:
That all the words after the word "regrets" in the amendment be struck out and the following substituted therefor;
That the government proposes further reductions in the income tax, this making a serious departure from the principle of direct taxation;
That the proposed revision of the customs tariff is inadequate to bring effective relief to the consuming public, and that the 6ales tax on the necessaries of life has not been eliminated.
I still believe, Mr. Speaker, that we were right in advocating that the income tax should not have been reduced, and right also in the position we took on the tariff. Therefore I intend to cast a vote along the same lines this year, and it must be against the budget.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OP THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would not get up at this time, Mr. Speaker, but for the fact that I would like to clarify somewhat the statement that has been made and reiterated so often in this debate regarding prosperity, which has been so vulgarly flaunted in the face of our farmers and agriculturists both in the speech from the throne and the budget debate.
The amendment which we are considering is a camouflaged pronouncement on the principle of protection and is meant to catch the unwary agriculturist. I do not think that any debate in any session of parliament since confederation has been equalled by this one for dissimulation or duplicity in argument. From the time the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) spoke, every member on the Tory side of this house has advocated protection as the one thing needful, *and has also in argument spoken of the Liberals as a free trade party and treated the government as though it had presented a free trade budget this year. They say that this budget is going to bring ruin to the industries of Canada. The truth is that both Liberal and Conservative parties in this house are high protectionists, and while both parties express concern for the agriculturists and for the industry of agriculture, not one of them cares one iota for the welfare of the farmer to-day, further than to trap him into asking for protection so that a valid excuse may be found, if possible, to increase the tariff on manufactured goods. Both parties know that

The Budget-Mr. Evans
agriculture in the United States to-day has been reduced to a state of penury through protection, Which is the ideal to be attained here-a state in which those in control of manufacturing, distribution, and the credit of the nation will have the rest of the population at their meTcy.
The Prime Minister declared that there was truth in the statement of the hon. member for South Wellington when he said that there was unbounded prosperity in this country. I want to say that both hon. gentlemen were *wrong. Either they made the statement in complete ignorance or with a desire to create a wrong impression. I received a letter from an old friend in Saskatchewan the other day, from the constituency of my hon. friend the member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell), which well clarifies the situation so far as prosperity for the working farmer in western Canada to-day is concerned. He says:
During the twenty-five years I have lived here. I do not think I have seen so many foreclosures and hardships. The oldtimers are nearly all losing their land. If I were to draw a plan of my township, I believe seventy-five per cent of the land has changed hands in the last year or so. In some cases the wife acquired the property from the mortgage company, and now it is the wife's turn to move. Yet we have never had a crop failure in the district. This year, of course, frost hit most pretty hard. How it is in some districts where they are subject to hail, drought, and so forth, it is hard to Imagine.
Saskatchewan to-day, Mr. Speaker, is in just the same position that compelled the government to appoint the Duncan commission to inquire into conditions in the maritime provinces. We need a Duncan commission to-day to inquire into conditions in agriculture in the west just as much as a commission was needed to inquire into conditions in the maritime provinces. The one concern of the government and of all protectionist interests throughout the country is to bring in from Europe and other parts of the world those who will take the place of the old settlers in this country, knowing that they can be more easily brought to accept a lower standard of living than is possible on the farms of Canada to-day. The statement that there is unbounded prosperity is reiterated for the purpose of trying to hide the iniquitous system of the concentrating of the earnings of the nation in the pockets of those who profit by acts of legislation giving a privilege to filch the earnings of the workers and agriculturists from their very pockets. Prosperity as boasted of in the budget is the result of the legalized brigandism for which both the government and the opposition are noted.
I was much struck with the speech of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). He struck a high note in the debate. He showed that wars were due to false trade policies. I am sure we are all glad to know of the nations' outlawing war by any and all means whatsoever. The hon. gentleman said that world peace will now depend on the subsequent actions of those nations who have put their names to the Kellogg treaty. He believed that trade restrictions and tariffs were the greatest cause of enmity between nations. Now, to hear a member of the government give utterance to such sentiments is in itself very gratifying. But at the time I could not help wondering how soon we could bring about world peace at the rate the Liberal government is moving towards free trade to-day.
The hon. gentleman said that Canada is competing and can compete with the world. The facts do not bear out his statement as far as urban industry goes. Not one industry in Canada to-day outside of agriculture has been able to stand on its own feet. Because of this system of protection the manufacturing industry and exchange of Canada are centred in the hands of a ring, and no business man who may be willing to come here and establish business on his own account, depending on his own industry and ability, has the slightest prospect of success unless he first of all links up with the politicians, or what may be termed the legislative faculty of the ring. If he does not do so, sooner or later he is put out of business. I can refer to several incidents to show that this is the case, and I do not need to tax my memory very far back. I have only to recall some incidents in our distributing system and our co-operative efforts and enterprises in western Canada to confirm my statement. I can remember when we intended opening a big wholesale house in Regina to supply our own needs; but we found out there and then that through the protectionist system of Canada we could not buy one dollar's worth of the commodities we needed, we could not under any circumstances enter the wholesale business in the city of Regina.

speechtext:
Is the hon. gentleman
able to point to any legislation :by the federal parliament which would prevent a man starting up a wholesale business anywhere in the Dominion? I think he has made an incorrect statement.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OP THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When we failed in Regina we thought we could open up a wholesale establishment in the great distributing centre of Winnipeg. We did so. How? We had to get another concern to buy for us. Both that
The Budget-Mr. Evans

concern and our own have been out of business for some years. This happened to Saskatchewan Grain Growers in their cooperative work.
Then what happened to the farmers of Ontario in their efforts along the same lines when they did not take care first of all to link up with the politicians in this house? When they could save two or three cents a pound on binder twine by getting it from Belfast they sent an order there. The shipment was held up in Montreal, and $30,000 was seized -all done with the idea of reducing the agriculturists of this countiy to a dependent state. That twine was afterwards released by the customs on payment of $6,000 in cash-stolen from the farmers of Ontario. Twine is on the free list. I want to show how free it is. Last year the consumers of Canada paid at least $555,000,000 because of this tariff system to put $185,000,000 into the Dominion treasury.
The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) says that by half a dozen strokes of the pen the Minister of Finance can cure the problem of unemployment. Like the member for Nanaimo (Mr. Dickie), he would stop the export of raw material. I am sure he would not dare to put such a policy into force were he in power. But he made the statement, forgetting that the class for whom last year this nation sweated to the extent of $555,000,000 because of the tariff do not even believe in their own policy of protection. I know what would cure unemployment in this country-the investment of capital for the exploitation of our natural resources. I obtained from the Bureau of Statistics figures showing that in 1927 our Canadian capitalists invested in foreign countries $1,330,586,000. This large sum of the people's earnings was invested abroad by a class who claim to have a monopoly of Canadian patriotism. Well, the hon. gentleman said nothing about patriotism.
I find from the magazine published by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company that those foreign investments increased during 1928 by over $330,000,000. The investment of this huge sum in the development of our resources would cure unemployment. But I say again, as I have said before when speaking for the farmers of Canada, the Canadian capitalists care nothing for the working men of their native country as long as they have a hungry crowd around the factory doors each morning seeking jobs. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) declared that our workers are living better than are the workers of any other country. This is not true. The average wage paid to our workers last year was $920-a wage far below the living line to-day.

The conditions of life on our Canadian farms are also of a very low standard, with heavy mortgages on the self-imposed slaves, and the landlord and tenant system with all its evils increasing each year. During the war the farmer's produce was commandeered at a price representing about 50 per cent of its value-less than 50 per cent compared with the sky-rocketed prices of those for whom our war debt was borrowed. Yet the government can relieve that class from payment of their just share of the national debt by making two successive reductions in the income tax in 1927 and 1928. If this boasted prosperity is so prevalent throughout the country, why does not the government now increase the income tax by making a sharper graduation in the scale?
The 1929 budget to my mind is simply a call for tenders in preparation for the next election. The slogan of the whole fiscal horoscope appears to be " For manufacturers' use only." The consumer is not relieved of any corresponding amount of the penalty he has to pay if he imports any goods made from the articles now placed on the free list or on the drawback list, which is increased again this year. No; this vulgar boast of prosperity, flaunted in the speech from the throne and now again in the budget speech, has reference only to the tariff filching propensities of this government, who are directing things at present. The government may well feel satisfied with its tariff filching propensities, but I would issue the warning: Don't call it prosperity. Surely there are means of finding revenue without putting the burden on the worker and his family-and the bigger the family the heavier the tariff penalty imposed is felt.
I would suggest to the government to-day to consider a sharp graduation in the income tax, and particularly should this be done to meet our war debt by the class for whom the war debt was incurred. We could meet our war debt to-day in an easy manner if all classes were taxed equitably, if an equitable method of taxation were found as between one class and another. Those who are making excess profits should pay a greater share than they are paying. We are allowing watered stock to be added to the capitalization of our concerns on which interest is expected to be paid, and a greater burden than ever is placed on the worker. Again, all unearned increment belongs to the community. I think a more sharply graduated inheritance tax would also furnish a good part of the revenue. While this is used to some extent by the provinces it is not used in Canada as it should be. The

The Budget-Division
most prolific means of taxation in Canada today is practically untouched, and that is land values, which would beyond any doubt furnish a large portion of our revenue. But as yet we prefer to follow the uncivilized method of taxing the food and clothing of the worker instead of the land of the rich which the worker has made valuable. Some reforms are needed along these lines, and I could not let this opportunity go without showing some of the abuses laid upon certain classes by other classes in the country, with the consent of this government.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OP THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am very much pleased
to be able to say something which draws applause from my hon. friends; I hope they may applaud me when I sit down.
My reason for presuming upon the indulgence of the house for a very few minutes, Mr. Speaker, is because I feel that there were many questions dealt with in this debate and many attitudes taken, particularly by the members of the government, which should be drawn to the attention of the people of this country. I think it is time the people of Canada should learn the policy of this government, or the lack of policy of this government, however we may put it, because at times it is difficult to know just for what policy this government stands.
I listened with a great deal of attention to previous speakers in this debate and particularly to the speeches of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice and my right hon. friend the Prime Minister; I hoped that perhaps they might give us something constructive and might offer something in the shape of a real Canadian policy which would be of benefit to this country in the days to come. But, Sir, I listened in vain; I hearo' nothing from any of the speakers on the other side of the house but vain boastings of a prosperity which is at least doubtful and certainly spotty. Certainly for such prosperity as does exist this government is no more responsible than I am responsible for the revolution of the planets.
Of course, at this late hour I do not intend to take very much time to deal with the remarks of the other speakers in this debate, but just for a few moments I wish to deal with one or two parts of the speech of the Prime Minister which illustrate the difficulty of depending very much upon that speech. My right hon. friend started off by pointing out that this country was very prosperous and he gave many figures to support that statement. Among the first figures he gave was the acreage under field crops in Canada; he said that in 1928 the acreage amounted to 59,351,000, or 3,000,000 acres more than in 1927. With that statement I shall not quarrel, but I would like to point out to the right hon. gentleman that if the acreage in field crops is a typical criterion of the prosperity of our country, then our country has not been prosperous since this government came into power. The Canada Year Book shows that the acreage in field crops in 1921 amounted to 59,635,000 or 300,000 acres,

The Budget-Mr. Manion
in round figures, more than the total acreage of last year, 1928. The figures in the Canada Year Book show that there have never since been as many acres in field crops as there were in 1921.
The right hon. gentleman used the word " deception " a number of times. He is usually very courteous, but I must confess that I thought he would be called to order by Your Honour. He used that word in referring to a number of speeches on this side of the house, and I think he came pretty close to political juggling if not deception when he gave the figures which he gave.
He also mentioned that this side of the house had thrown overboard the word " protection," but in the amendment upon which we voted a few moments ago there appear the words " safeguard and protect." It is quite true that the word "safeguard" is not used very much in Canada, but I would like to know just when it has become a crime to use a good British word here in Canada. While we may have neglected on some occasions to put in the word " protection " we have always advocated protection and, when we were in power we always lived up to the principle of protection; but what must we think of a party which when in or out of office have preached a policy of free trade and ever afterwards practise protection?
The right hon. gentleman said, as he has said before, that we should have conscripted the wealth of the country. That may be a little touch of demagogism, but he pointed out in his speech, as he has in many others, that we did not put on sufficient taxes during the war. I would like to quote three or four lines from a little book I have in my hand entitled English Public Finances. This was published in 1920 by the Bankers Trust Company of New York City, so I hardly think the right hon. gentleman can object to it. This book deals with the public finances of Britain from the early days of the Norman conquest right up to the present time. In dealing with Great Britain in particular, the article says:
For the active war period covering the five fiscal years ending March 31, 1919, from 22J per cent to 34i per cent of the expenditure was raised from taxation, other revenue collections, and war contributions.
In referring to the dominions, it says:
The dominions have made an equally good or even better showing. Canada has taxed herself for nearly fifty per cent (48.10) of her total war time expenditure; Australia raised 40 per cent from taxation and New Zealand appears to have raised 57 per cent from taxation.
In view of those figures I hope the right hon. gentleman will hesitate about making similar statements in the future.

speechtext:
My hon. friends seem to be cheering me as easily as they cheered some of their own speakers. The right hon. gentleman said in his speech:
May I say that I can conceive of no greater misfortune than that the question of the St. Lawrence waterway should be mixed up in any way with the question of the tariff of this country or of the United States. Each question must be dealt with separately on its merits.
In replying to a question of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) he proceeded to read the letter which had been forwarded to the government of the United States. In part, this letter reads:
In this connection, it may be said that Canadian agriculture is more directly affected by the restrictions on the importation of Canadian farm products, which have been imposed by the United States in recent years, with the object, it is understood, of assisting agriculture in those western states which would share so largely in the benefits of the proposed St. Lawrence waterway. This situation, and the effects upon the maritime sections of Canada of United States duties on the products of the fisheries, are among the factors which have contributed to bringing it about that public opinion in Canada has not so clearly crystallized in favour of the waterway project as appears to be the case in the United States.
I would like to ask the right hon. gentleman if that is a species of self-hypnotism.
The Budget-Mr. Manion

speechtext:
All I can say, Mr. Speaker, is that if the Prime Minister was in a hypnotic trance when he quoted that letter, he certainly has not come out of that trance yet. If that was not self-hypnotism, then it was self-deception; it was sophistry of the worst kind, if it was not just ordinary poiitical humbug. What attention will the people of this country pay to the words of the right non. gentleman when he contradicts himself like that?
Then he said that we should conscript the wealth of this country in the next war, not only conscript the wealth but conscript all other things.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OP THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, no.

speechtext: I have not the time to look it up, but I remember the expression very well. I am very glad the right hon. gentleman has a policy for the next war, because he did not have very much of a policy for the last one. The trouble with the Prime Minister is that he becomes too enthusiastic after an event, rather than before. I do not like that expression of conscripting the wealth, and I do not think it would be feasible, but so far as the conscripting of the services of all our people is concerned, if another war should unhappily come upon us, I am just as strong for that as is the right hon. the Prime Minister. I feel that all people should serve, but when the Prime Minister sets a course like that I am afraid he is likely to steer away from that chart when the time comes.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OP THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about the conscripting of wheat in the last war?

speechtext:
I will let my hon. friend
deal with that next year. I have enough points against the government; in fact, I have: so many I cannot begin to exhaust them all in fifteen or twenty minutes and I do not intend to speak any longer.
A couple of words which I used in my speech seem to have caused a good deal of antagonism on the part of my hon. friends.
I do not know why they should have taken umbrage as they did, but I used the words "red-blooded Canadian policy." I did not assail the United States, and I do not assail the United States now. I like the United States, but I love Canada. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), in dealing with that-and I found myself laughing a little 
when he came to the words "red-blooded," because I thought he would not conclude his speech without referring to them-said that it was not "red blood" we needed but "cool heads". The difficulty with the Prime Minister is that he has his extremities mixed. It is not a cool head that is troubling this government; it is cold feet that is troubling them, and if he had studied physiology in his youth as I did, he would realize that in both matters, not only to warm up the feet, but to cool down the head, you need red blood anyhow, and they need it on both counts.
My hon. friends from the prairies will remember there are trains out there that go out empty in order to come back full. They are what we call deadhead trains. I would like to remind the Prime Minister that the coolest kind of a head is a deadhead, and the trouble with the government is that it is a deadhead government-nothing but platitudes and no policies.
I listened with great attention to both the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) who usually make interesting speeches. I have heard the Minister of Justice making what I consider witty and brilliant speeches in the house, but his last speech was not up to the mark. Yesterday in reply to one of my friends, the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Boys), the Minister of Justice suggested that he would like to have finished his speech. We all realize that he had not finished it, because when he was talking, he did not get anywhere; he did not have any terminal facilities. The hon. gentleman, in coming to a lot of theoretical conclusions and getting nowhere practically, made me think of a remark of the Hon. Mr. Harcourt who, speaking of one of his colleagues, said that the trouble was he was a brilliant enough fellow but he lacked that vulgar quality of common sense. I am afraid that is what the speech of the Minister of Justice lacked the other day.

speechtext: Order.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OP THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not say that with any disrespect. What was the gist of the speech of the Minister of Justice? The entire speech was that an abstract resolution carried by a group of men at Geneva a couple of years ago, Should be the whole basis of policy in the Dominion of Canada. He forgot, for example, that the whole United States press- and I read much of it at the time-criticized their representatives for having |put their names to such a resolution. He also forgot, when he read the names of the five members who represented Canada, that not one of those members had ever been, so far as I know,

The Budget-Mr. Manion
elected to a representative body in this country. I am not saying this in disrespect of their capabilities; but they had not been up against practical problems; they had been dealing with theoretical questions all their lives. They agreed to a theoretical proposition, and now the Minister of Justice says that his complaint against us is that we do not agree with this resolution; that we have not put this into force to a greater extent. As a matter of fact, he pointed out himself that the only country in the world that had put this into force was Canada. Even free trade England never put it into force. Since the war, free-trade England, the only country that for a hundred years has practised free trade, has been putting up tariff barriers under the term of safeguarding industries. We have been the only country who have dared to reduce our tariffs to any extent at all, thereby killing our own trade and increasing that of the United States. This reminds me of the story of the old mother who was watching a regiment passing and who said: "They are all out of step but our Jimmy."

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OP THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is not new.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OP THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I know, but I want to use it with relation to the members of the Liberal party. They think all the ministers of finance throughout the world are out of step except their Jim. They forget that the tariff is a weapon by which we can negotiate with other countries for trade favours, and we alone have thrown away our weapons. It is a weapon which has been used by all countries in the world. But it has not been used by this country because in practically every trade treaty we have made with other countries, we have suffered. The strange thing of it all is that the Minister of Justice, who is a pet son of the province of Quebec-and I have no complaint in that regard-who has always been a favourite son of Quebec, is so indifferent to that province that loves him so much that he prefers Geneva to Quebec.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OP THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

speechtext:
Why, the hon. member
for North Simcoe yesterday in the house, in a very able speech, read a resolution which was passed unanimously on March 27 in the provincial legislature of Quebec, after Mr. Taschereau agreed to withdraw his motion to go into committee of supply. That resolution which they agreed to unanimously was entirely a protective resolution; every word of it was protective.
And, how did the Prime Minister deal with the speech of the Minister of Justice? How did he take this attitude on trade policies? He left Geneva and, by the way, this was a 78594-94
great government to travel. If they cannot travel in private cars or trains, they travel in automobiles all over Europe, and when the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) is taunted with it, he says: "What have you got to say about it?" That is his attitude. But the Prime Minister left Geneva and went across to Washington for his policy. He says: " We have to be very careful in regard to our whole policy at the present time or we will provoke Washington." That is a sort of policy,,whereby we must not do anything; we must take an attitude whereby by no word of ours should we seem to have any opinions of our own at all. I have heard a great deal of abuse of the word " retaliation," I do not know why; it seems a good enough word, but I am not using it because some hon. members do not seem to like it. But the Prime Minister seemed to think that if anybody used the word " retaliation," it was almost a crime, rendering one liable to go to gaol; that if anybody talked about British preference, there was a danger of provoking Washington; that we should have a sort of " sit quiet, hush-hush " policy. The trouble with this government has been that it has been a " hush-hush " government with regard to any policy that would build up Canada. Since 1925 there have been travelling throughout the country the leader of the opposition-

speechtext: The leader of the government.

speechtext:
The leader of the government. It is only a little time until the leader of the opposition will be leader of the government, so my mistake is one only of time and not of intent. The leader of the government and the Minister of Justice have been travelling from end to end of Canada, talking about this magnificent status to which we have attained, this wonderful status of Canada. They say that they have broadened out our whole status; that we have become a real nation. What kind of a status is it when we do not even dare to call our souls our own? What kind of status have we attained when we do not dare to do anything but practise a " hush-hush " policy, no matter what the United States says or does. We are a proud nation, it seems to me, but under the leadership of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice we have attained to that great position where it is advocated by the Minister of Justice that we take our policies from Geneva and by the Prime Minister that we take our policies from Washington. Mr. Speaker, the members on this side of the house believe in taking their policies from Ottawa. Canada.

What kind of leadership are we getting in this country from a government that talks of free trade, in theory, on the hustings throughout the country, but, in practice, in the house puts into force a protective policy? What kind of leadership is it which advocates senate reform when it is on the hustings and out of power, but stands for senate stability when it is seated in this house? What kind of leadership is it that spends millions on the decoration and beautification of the city of Ottawa, but has not one dollar for technical education or national highways? What kind of leadership is it that permits for lack of a proper immigration policy thousands of Europeans to come into our country and drives out, by lack of a Canadian policy, the same number of Canadians to the United States? What kind of leadership is it that builds up United States industries and destroys Canadian industries? What kind of leadership is it that has no word of support or protection for the dairy and fruit industries of this country, but builds up the dairy and fruit industries of other lands? What kind of leadership is it that says we must not mix up the tariff and the St. Lawrence questions, and then proceeds to make a salad of the two? speechtext:
But to continue with my
quotation:
In representing Canada for these purposes the Prime Minister, we believe, is expressing the unanimous desire of the Canadian people to seek by all possible means the establishment of an ordered and peaceful world society and the substitution for war of arbitration, conciliation and conference.
This is what the most eminent man in the Conservative party, the only living man in that party who has won general elections, declares. This is what Sir Robert Borden says, now that he has left active polities and is enjoying the quiet of private life in Ottawa, in a position to study the great problems that affect our country. He has no prejudices; he has no longer any interest in the

The Budget-Mr. Pouliot
welfare of his party but is concerned about the future of this country which we a'l cherish. And if he were in the house now he would be silent instead of being noisy, like hon. gentlemen who prefer noise to argument. He stands out as the great figure of the Conservative party, a man personally above all reproach. And what does he say? He says that the Prime Minister of this country (Mr. Mackenzie King) is doing his best for Canada.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OP THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon.
friend from Fort William spoke of political juggling, and I noticed when he spoke that he was doing his daily dozen before dinner. He spoke of the many attitudes taken by the members of the government and said, "I am not responsible for the revolution of the planets." I do not say that he is a wandering star in the Tory constellation, but he is responsible for his own evolutions, because he had two distinct policies in 1917. He was then a Laurier Liberal and afterwards a Unionist. He spoke of the lack of leadership and qualified this as a deadhead government. The Tory party is a hydra, a seven-headed monster; there are nearly as many leaders in that party as there are front seats on that side of the house.
Then my hon. friend referred to the fact that many members of the cabinet went to the United States during the Easter recess, and at the same time he spoke of cold feet. Yet he saj^s he likes the United States; ignoti mulla cupido, he could not like that country without knowing it. Although he reproached the members of the government for going to the United States he went there himself during the Easter recess in order to get his cold feet sunburned. He was surprised that the Prime Minister was not called to order for using the word "deception" while referring to speeches made by Tory members. If the word "deception," like truth, hurts so much, does my hon. friend think the Prime Minister should have used instead the expression "sour grapes"?
There are two kinds of governments; there is the government of the people, by the people and for the people, which is the Liberal government, and there is the government for the few privileged classes, which is the Tory government. On this side of the house the
Liberal party has a red-blooded Canadian policy; on the other side of the house the Tory party has a blue-blooded class policy. My hon. friend said he did not like the expression "conscription of wealth" but he is willing to conscript the services of the people.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OP THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Conscript them all, Frenchmen and everyone.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OP THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Hon. gentleman opposite
do not like the conscription of wealth because they are a capitalistic party looking after capitalistic interests and hoping for a capitalistic future. The hon. member for Fort William approved the issue by the Tory government of victory bonds free from income tax. This was not conscription of wealth but far from it; it gave an opportunity to people who were well off to buy large quantities of victory bonds of that kind and- escape the payment of income tax. In that way the rich Tory lords evaded taxation.

one question? Is it not a fact, that the issuance of tax-free victory bonds was approved unanimously by the house?

Perhaps I might ask my
hon. friend a question also: Is he one of the wealthy Tory lords who enjoyed that benefit?

speechtext: Then I do not understand how my hon. friend can be a Conservative; he should be a Liberal. It is not a fact that the bankers' trust had for sale an issue of Canadian tax-free victory bonds and that they stated Canada was heavily taxed in order to have a better opportunity to sell those bonds?

friend knows that all the municipal bond issues in the United States are exempt from income tax?

speechtext:
This is just another instance where hon. gentlemen opposite, who complain very much because we are friendly with the United States instead of being at war with them, quote the United States as an example for Canada.
My hon. friend from Fort William said that the Minister of Justice did not finish his speech. He did not do so because of the interruptions of a member on the other side of the house, so why should he be reproached
The Budget-Mr. Pouliot

because he was unable to conclude his remarks? Then my hon. friend said the Minister of Justice was disloyal to his own province, but that assertion does not stand for a moment. The Minister of Justice stands very high in Quebec; I am proud of his accomplishments, and moreover I used his name in my county when Mr. Patenaude was bringing in his policy of nothing.
We all heard the Prime Minister say that the tariff policy of this country has been and always will be decided in Ottawa, and that is the course which will be pursued by the Liberal party. This afternoon the hon. member for Fort William was quoting Senator Borah and a banker named Fiske in the United States, and to-night his leader quotes the municipalities of that country as an example for us. This is the dessert after dinner.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OP THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Tell us about
Taschereau.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OP THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friends opposite
tell me to speak about the Premier of Quebec, but I will not do so to-night because I have no orders to take from hon. gentlemen opposite. To use the expression of the hon. member for Fort William it would be a kind of disappointment.
May I say this about the resolution which has been passed by the Quebec assembly; there are three kinds of protection, high protection, moderate protection and low protection.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OP THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And Liberal protection.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OP THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When our friends speak of protection they do not say whether they mean high protection, moderate protection or low protection. High protection protects the capitalists only, the money lords of this country, while moderate protection is of benefit to the manufacturer as well as to the consumer. That is the policy which has always been advocated by this party, but our friends do not say just what kind of protection they want to have; they do not say whether they want protection for the rich or for the poor.
The acreage in field crops is not the only criterion of prosperity. The banks are boasting of the prosperity in this country.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OP THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And Premier Taschereau.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OP THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And the Seven Sisters.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
