speechtext: Order.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OP THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Premier Taschereau can boast of prosperity because he is a financier himself. He is a director of the Sun Life Assurance Company, the Metropolitan Life, Barclay's bank, and a savings bank in Quebec. He is very wel acquainted with business conditions, and when he says the country is prosperous, at least he must be prosperous himself. The banks are boasting of the prosperity of this country, and so are the financiers. Even the member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) is boasting of prosperity; he said that his business is prosperous. The heads of the great railways, the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railway, are also boasting of prosperity. AVhen this government boasts of prosperity it is only repeating what is said by the men who know the true state of affairs. When any member says that the government is killing our trade he only shows that he is, not a disappointed, but a "sour grapes" politician.
Low prices are sometimes caused through there being a better harvest than in previous years, but the policy of this government has always been the policy of government of the people, by the people and for the people. Before recess, and with regard to Geneva, I mentioned what Sir Robert Borden had said. An article appears in to-day's five o'clock edition of the Ottawa Journal, which gives an interview with Sir Robert Borden who had just returned from a two months' visit to the United States. He stayed there longer than the hon. member for Fort William, so he should know of the conditions prevailing there. Sir Robert Borden has had more experience in the government of this country than any hon. member on the other side, and the article, which appears on the front page of this newspaper, reads:
A few days were spent in New York, where Sir Robert had the privilege of meeting at dinner a gathering comprising many men very prominent in finance, industry and transportation. He was particularly impressed with their friendly attitude and with their warm appreciation of Canadian development, progress and institutions.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OP THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Dispense.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OP THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The article continues:
"Without exception," said Sir Robert, "they evinced the utmost faith in the future of our Dominion, and emphasized its abundant resources. A leading New York banker spoke with great admiration of our banking system and of its remarkable success.
The vice-president of a very important railway commented on the fact that in Canada we had practically only two railway systems while in the United States there are more than one hundred, and he expressed the opinion that Canada in this respect occupied a more advantageous position than the United States. He

The Budget-Mr. Pouhot
spoke also of the excellent organization and service of both the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National Railways. Keen interest was evinced in the remarkable development of electrical energy in Canada and the mineral development in the northern portions of Quebec, Ontario and Manitoba."
As my hon. friends have asked me to talk about matters pertaining to Quebec, I will read from a Tory paper of Quebec, the Chronicle-Telegraph of April 8, which has the following to say about the Conservative party:
Campaign Afoot to Split up Federal Conservative Party and divide the Leadership
Cahan is Named as the Sectional Leader
That a subtle campaign is now on foot to split the federal Conservative party, and create in the province of Quebec what may be descibed as a Nationalist-Conservative wing, with Mr. C. H. Cahan, member for St. Lawrence, in the saddle-
I suppose that refers to the dark horse. The article continues:
-to divide control with the Hon. R. B. Bennett, appears to be substantiated following the discovery of an underground movement, engineered within the province, and sponsored delicately by some sections of the so-called provincial Conservative press.
Already the movement has gone so far as to nominate delegates, agreeable to the proposal, to attend a convention to be held in Montreal in the near future, at which it is presumed tangible shape will be given to the scheme. Absolutely no authority for any such convention has been given by the federal Conservative organization, it is claimed, and if this is the case, there is no alternative but to believe that the project is a deliberate attempt to split the party on racial lines, with the province of Quebec playing an isolated and it is hoped dominant role, in the prospective destiny of the Conservative party at Ottawa.
I do not know on which side they will be when they are called upon to give their opinion. The article concludes:
The genesis of the trouble in the Conservative party goes back to the Winnipeg convention when the leadership of the party went to Mr. Bennett in preference to Mr. Cahan. Mr. Cahan no doubt believed he had a legitimate title to leadership and a change came over his attitude in the federal house which the French press or sections of it were not slow to note. From the "Mail and Empire", Toronto. came the news that the member for St. Lawrence was in actual revolt against his party. If his activity in fighting the federal Liberal party was unabated, it was felt that it was out of no love for his chief Mr. R. B. Bennett.
I think I like his chief more than he does.
It is no secret that the Conservatives of the province have for some time been dissatisfied with the treatment the party headquarters meted out to them and the stage seemed all set for a split.
A curious procedure then followed. Reorganization of the party in the province has long been necessary. But the means adopted are, to say the least of it, distinctly odd.
It is understood that Mr. J. L. Gauthier, an ex-candidate for Dorchester, has been busying himself in the matter. It is known that he has gone through the province arranging meetings of Conservatives and Quebec was one of the places visited. His business, it is understood, was to have delegates appointed from the various constituencies in the province who would attend a convention in Montreal in the near future, and the question is being asked what the business of this gathering will be.
To Create Schisms
At any rate other leaders of the party are apparently convinced that he has no good intention in the matter and have circularized the delegates thus appointed with various pointed questions. "Did Mr. Gauthrier say who gave him the mandate for acting so and what is the aim of this convention?" they are asked.
Continuing the circular letter points out that its writers are convinced that Mr. Gauthier had no mandate from Mr. Bennett nor from General McRae-
In a local theatre there is a play called Mother Machree where Belle Bennett plays a leading role. Mother Machree is a hen which has been breeding ducks.

chief organizer for the Dominion, and that this so-called convention has in reality a hostile object to Mr. Bennett. They believe the aim is to appoint a Conservative chief in the province who will be in a position to dictate to the leader or create a schism in the Conservative ranks which would do irreparable damage to the party.
The damage is already done.
The pro-Bennett Conservatives apparently believe that the provincial leader is to play something of the role of a king-maker-
We have our own King and we made him what he is. We are proud of his accomplishments.
-or at least dictate to the legitimate chief just how he must act.
In view of the existing situation it is believed that General McRae will shortly visit Quebec to conduct an elaborate investigation of the whole matter

Hear, hear.
-ascertain just how far the movement has gone and naturally attempt at all cost to preserve the integrity of his party and prevent the formation of anything in the nature of an independent provincial Nationalist-Conservative party.
Cryptic Editorials
Cryptic editorials have recently appeared in the local press which readers have been at some difficulty to understand. For example a recent editorial-
It must be an editorial in L'Evenement, a Tory French paper published in Quebec.
14S4
The Budget-Mr. Pouliot

-points out that while the Conservatives in this province do not disown Mr. Meighen's successor (Mr. Bennett) they have a tendency to follow the leadership of the member for St. Lawrence who is characterized as the possessor of a legitimate ambition with important financial backing.
Important financial backing.
The editorial continues that to assure the success of this manifestation a provincial convention will be held in Montreal in April.
It will be called the Montreal convention.
The convention is to be a replica of the Winnipeg convention, only on a provincial scale and Mr. Cahan is to be rewarded for the goodwill he showed in vindicating the rights of the French minority.
The hon. member for St. Lawrenee-St. George, is to be rewarded, like old man Simeon, before his death.
Continuing, it is pointed out that the aim of the convention is to invest Mr. Cahan with the high command of the Conservative forces in the province of Quebec so that Mr. Cahan can in future speak to Mr. Bennett-
Apparently he does not speak to him now.
*-and dictate to him the conditions of a Tory alliance. Mr. Cahan has given no indication of his position in the matter but these chiefs of the Conservative party are apparently apprehensive of a schism in the party

What is the matter with these chiefs of the the Conservative party?
-and wish to nip the project in the bud.
I am proud to be on friendly terms with the leader of the opposition; I respect him very much as an individual; I think he is well fitted for the position, and I believe he will be leader of the opposition in this house as long as he wishes to be here, provided that he is elected in his constituencj'.
May I recall to you, Mr. Speaker, the fact that for four generations members of my family have been in this house. My great granfather stood for responsible government and against the family compact. My grandfather supported Blake, Mackenzie, Dorion; my father recommended you, sir, to Sir Wilfrid Laurier, as member for Gaspe, and it was a very happy selection. They have all done their duty. I consider that I am the servant of the people; I do not care for the wealthy; I am the representative of the people who are the majority; they are the people who suffer and who struggle when the Tories are in power. When this party is in power it is a government of the people, for the people and by the people, and they are glad to support it.
There is another difference between the Liberal party and the Conservative party. The Conservative party is the party of the

few, where everyone expects to be a chieftain; but in the Liberal party we do not try to favour this one or that one; we try to do justice to all, and this is what has been done by the government since it has come into power. We are very proud of our Prime Minister and of his distinguished colleagues in the cabinet.
My hon. friend's speech will not help the Conservative party in any way; the Conservative party does not know how mucn damage it will suffer from such a speech, because the people outside of this house are not fools. They grasp the arguments and if they will read the resume of a speech like that of my hon. friend, they will find only words and not a single argument except two ridiculous quotations from Senator Borah of Idaho and a Mr. Fi^ke, of New York City.
Mr. Speaker, my last word is this: the Liberal party is strong in the province of Quebec to-day and it will come out stronger and stronger after the general election takes place-I do not know when. I shall not be sorry for them then, but those on the other side of the house who scream to-day will no longer retain their seats. There will be fewer Conservatives returned. The people of this country do not appreciate those appeals to prejudice. They do not appreciate the. appeals of the hon. gentleman from Fort William who goes to New York and dares to complain because other hon. gentlemen go there. This is a very trifling matter, and I never thought that a man of high culture like my hon. friend would use such matter in his speech. It is the Conservatives that will be the losers on account of such appeals. The people in the country will realize as we realize in this house that there is nothing in their speeches but gross insult.

Buffer.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I desire to ask the minister a question with respect to this matter. On page 5 of the report dated January 5, 1928, of Mr. Moore, Chairman of the Advisory Board on Tariff and Taxation, I find these words:
As was perhaps to be expected from a comparatively new departure in government, some question has been raised as to the boards' functions. As set forth by order in council, April 7, 1926, (P.C. 530).
"The duties of the board are to inquire into and hear representations on all matters pertaining to the tariff and other forms of taxation, as may be directed by the Minister of Finance, and to advise the minister in regard thereto."
Little difficulty has been experienced as to the duty of inquiry. Possibly we might have succeeded better proceeding under a set of questions stated by you, outlining the scope of the investigation, but we believe that on the whole our duty of inquiry has been discharged with reasonable satisfaction. Difficulty, however, exists as to determining the nature of the advice we are presumed by order in council to tender to the minister.
Applications in regard to customs invariably contain submission of evidence with the object of obtaining relief, whether by upward or downward revision of the tariff.
Parliament alone can grant that relief.
What then becomes the nature of the advice expected from the board? Is it for the board to express an opinion that the relief in question should or should not be given? If this be not its function, then is it possible for the board 78594-95
to report its opinion as to the extent to which the reasons urged for relief have been established, without reference or inference bearing upon the justification for relief.
The board has no desire to avoid responsibility. The board has a sincere desire to make its work helpful through you to parliament.
How best, then, may the board convey to you the information which it has received as a result of its investigations? As has been stated, verbatim reports are taken of the proceedings at public hearings. The transcripts will generally be found to contain much evidence helpful in the construction of tariff items in respect to their subject-matter. Reports of the inquiry into the major references, and some of the minor as well, are lengthy, and at times somewhat involved, usually containing valuable statistical matter. To present the evidence in precise form, possesses the advantage of brevity-and the disadvantage of incompleteness.
Then he proceeds about the arguments. was based upon a recommendation made by the tariff board. That recommendation should be in writing. That recommendation should be before this parliament. That recommendation should be available to every member of this house. Otherwise, we have substituted for governmental responsibility two or three gentlemen-it was three at first; then one ran off to Manitoba to run an election for hon. gentlemen opposite and he has become a part of the administration in that province, leaving the chairman, who, with one other, considered some of the most important matters affecting western Canada without western Canada having any representative on the board. And now secret advice is to be tendered-nothing open-nothing written. All we have is the word of the minister, which is always beyond question, but his word is based solely on his memory as to the advice tendered him by this board. In the light of the statement made by the chairman of the board himself, that is not the function of the board.
Have we a report from the tariff board this year? I have not seen it yet. The last report I have seen was dated January, 1928. We have no report before the house for the calendar year 1928, and yet we are asked to proceed to a discussion of these tariff items and arrive at conclusions with respect to them, not having before us any report made by that body which cost this country so much money last year. I ask the minister if that is his idea. Does he want us to think that? I am sure he does not. I am sure that he intends that we should have before us the report of the tariff board in writing. I have seen no report brought down this year, and I do submit that it is time we had it. I would ask the minister when we may expect it. I had made a note to ask him that question on the orders of the day some days ago, but I failed to ask him. The report for 1928 has not been tabled, I think. The only one tabled, so far as I have been able to ascertain, is the one which I have in my hand, which is for a period of time ending January, 1928. Is it proposed that we shall have the report from the chairman of the tariff board, and that the report shall be printed and made available to the members of the house before we consider the tariff changes that the minister proposes? If that report is not available to us, I ask the minister why he talks about this board at all. It becomes then, I will not say a secret tribunal, but a public tribunal that is tendering secret advice. That is not what the Canadian people expect from a tariff board. This is not a hole-in-the-corner business of which

the minister used to talk. He used to complain of people affected coming to Ottawa and meeting the minister and making representations with regard to their particular industries, but is that any worse than the farce and hypocrisy of a tribunal that hears evidence publicly and tenders advice secretly?
The minister says that the members of the board are his servants. That is not the idea of the Canadian people. That was not in the mind of Sir Thomas White when he introduced his bill providing for the appointment of a tariff board, the bill that was killed in the senate. The purpose was to have a tribunal clothed with powerful functions, that the Canadian people should have a tribunal beyond suspicion, not men looking for office, looking to their own election in Manitoba or Ontario, not men who were concerned about their own political fortunes, but men who would sit in a judicial capacity and adjudicate and determine and make written recommendations in which the Canadian people would have some confidence and upon which the minister might act with confidence. The minister has before him nothing more than a limited knowledge of this whole transaction, and he hopes to get all his proposals through simply by saying: "All these changes are made on the recommendations of the tariff board. I do not know who Dodwell and Company are, or who Mr. Deaohman is, or the consumers' league, but I called them in, and they sat in my office. I heard their recommendations, and I ask you to accept these changes." That is not discharging the functions of the minister; that is not discharging the functions of the tariff board.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:

Mr. STEVENS I did not make that statement.
Mr. ROBB That was the implication.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speechtext:
Because he takes up

Bringing out the evidence.

For the life of me I cannot see why my hon. friends on the other side should object if the manufacturer is assisted, unless they accuse us of inconsistency in so assisting the manufacturer; but I see no inconsistency at all in our attitude. Evidence showed that there were in the United States nearly one hundred crayon companies and, therefore, the industry in that country was highly competitive. It is the case, therefore, that the application of the Canada Crayon Company Limited cannot be said to have been fully dealt with until the applications involving colours and paraffin wax have been disposed of.
